Durance means imprisonment — specifically, being forcibly confined or held captive, often for a long period and under harsh or degrading conditions.

It is not just any temporary detention. The word carries a sense of prolonged, oppressive captivity — the kind where someone is locked away and has no freedom whatsoever.
How it feels compared to similar words

You already know words like imprisonment, captivity, and confinement. Durance means the same thing, but it is a much older, more literary word. You will almost never hear it in everyday conversation today. It lives in old poetry, classic novels, historical writing, and dramatic prose. When a modern writer uses it, they are deliberately reaching for an old, weighty, almost solemn feel — as if the word itself carries the heaviness of a dungeon.
The phrase you will almost always see it in

Durance almost never appears alone in modern writing. Instead, you will most commonly encounter it in the famous phrase:

"in durance vile"

Here, vile means wretched, degrading, or miserable. So the full phrase means: held in harsh, degrading captivity — not just imprisoned, but imprisoned under awful, humiliating conditions.

For example: "The prisoner languished in durance vile for years, forgotten by the world."

This phrase has been used by writers for centuries to describe miserable confinement, and it became so set that most people today only know durance through this fixed expression.

The important thing to understand is the emotional weight durance carries. It does not describe a quick arrest or a short jail stay. It suggests:

  • Prolonged confinement — you are held for a long time
  • Powerlessness — you cannot leave; your freedom is completely taken from you
  • Often, wretchedness — especially in the phrase "durance vile," the conditions are harsh and dehumanizing

You will encounter durance in:

  • Old English and Scottish poetry (it was common in Elizabethan and Jacobean writing)
  • 18th and 19th century novels
  • Historical writing about feudal or medieval imprisonment
  • Modern writing that deliberately mimics an archaic style, or that uses the phrase "durance vile" for dramatic or ironic effect

It is rare enough that when you see it, it stands out. A writer reaching for durance instead of imprisonment is making a very deliberate stylistic choice — they want to evoke something old, severe, and literary.

Think of someone locked in a cold stone cell, kept there for years on end, utterly powerless. That grim, lingering captivity — that is durance. And if those conditions are also degrading and wretched, that is durance vile.

• After the rebellion failed, the duke was thrown into durance and never seen in public again.
  • She joked that her nine-to-five desk job felt like durance vile.
  • The knight endured two years of durance in a foreign prison before his ransom was paid.

The last example is a good reminder: durance does not require a formal charge or legal process. It just requires being held captive against your will, unable to leave.

In one sentence: Durance means forced, prolonged captivity or imprisonment — and in its most famous use, "durance vile," it describes such captivity under wretched, degrading conditions.
